questions.worked_solution:
We start by integrating the velocity to get $x(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int {sec}^{2}⁡(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡(t)+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $x(\frac{\pi }{4})=2.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2 & =\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})+C \\ 2 & =1+C \\ C & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the position $x$ of the particle at time $t$ is 

$$
x(t)=\operatorname{tan}⁡(t)+1.
$$

questions.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with velocity $v(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),$ where $t$ is the time. If the particle is at the position $x=3$ when $t=0,$ calculate the position $x$ of the particle at time $t>0.$
questions.worked_solution:
We start by integrating the velocity to get $x(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $x(0)=3.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}3 & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(0))+C \\ 3 & =-\frac{1}{2}+C \\ C & =\frac{7}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the position $x$ of the particle at time $t$ is

$$
x(t)=\frac{7}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t).
$$

questions.problem:
A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration 

$$
a(t)=\frac{3}{\sqrt{t+1}},
$$

where $t\ge 0$ is the time. If the particle has position $x=4$ and velocity $v=-6$ when $t=0,$ the position $x$ of the particle at time $t$ is

$x(t)=$
{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
We start by integrating the acceleration to get the velocity $v(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int \frac{3}{\sqrt{t+1}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =3\int (t+1)^{-1/2}\,\text{d}t \\  & =3\cdot \frac{(t+1)^{1/2}}{1/2}+C \\  & =6\sqrt{t+1}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(0)=-6.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-6 & =6\sqrt{1}+C \\ -6 & =6+C \\ C & =-12.\end{aligned}
$$

So the velocity is given by 

$$
v(t)=6\sqrt{t+1}-12.
$$

Now, we integrate the velocity to get $x(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int (6\sqrt{t+1}-12)\,\text{d}t \\  & =6\int (t+1)^{1/2}\,\text{d}t-12\int \,\text{d}t \\  & =6\cdot \frac{(t+1)^{3/2}}{3/2}-12t+K \\  & =4(t+1)^{3/2}-12t+K.\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $K,$ we use the fact that $x(0)=4.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}4 & =4(1)^{3/2}-0+K \\ 4 & =4+K \\ K & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the position $x$ of the particle at time $t$ is 

$$
x(t)=4(t+1)^{3/2}-12t.
$$

questions.problem:
A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration $a(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),$ where $t\ge 0$ is the time. If the particle has position $x=0$ and velocity $v=1$ when $t=0,$ the position $x$ of the particle at time $t$ is

$x(t)=$
{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
We start by integrating the acceleration to get the velocity $v(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(0)=1.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)+C \\ 1 & =-\frac{1}{2}+C \\ C & =\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

So the velocity is given by $v(t)=-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\frac{3}{2}.$

Now, we integrate the velocity to get $x(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int (-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\frac{3}{2})\,\text{d}t \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t+\frac{3}{2}\int \,\text{d}t \\  & =-\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+\frac{3}{2}t+K\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $K$, we use the fact that $x(0)=0.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =-\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)+\frac{3}{2}(0)+K \\ K & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the position $x$ of the particle at time $t$ is 

$$
x(t)=-\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+\frac{3}{2}t.
$$

questions.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration $a(t)=6t+9{t}^{2}$, where $t\ge 0$ is the time. If the particle has position $x=2$ and velocity $v=6$ when $t=1$, calculate the position $x$ of the particle at time $t>0.$
questions.worked_solution:
We start by integrating the acceleration to get the velocity $v(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int (6t+9{t}^{2})\,\text{d}t \\  & =3{t}^{2}+3{t}^{3}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(1)=6.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}6 & =3(1)^{2}+3(1)^{3}+C \\ 6 & =6+C \\ C & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So the velocity is given by $v(t)=3{t}^{2}+3{t}^{3}.$ 

Now, we integrate the velocity to get $x(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int (3{t}^{2}+3{t}^{3})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={t}^{3}+\frac{3}{4}{t}^{4}+K\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $K$, we use the fact that $x(1)=2.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2 & =(1)^{3}+\frac{3}{4}(1)^{4}+K \\ 2 & =\frac{7}{4}+K \\ K & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the position $x$ of the particle at time $t$ is 

$$
x(t)={t}^{3}+\frac{3}{4}{t}^{4}+\frac{1}{4}.
$$

questions.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration $a(t)=4{e}^{4t}$, where $t\ge 0$ is the time. If the particle has position $x=\frac{1}{2}$ and velocity $v=1$ when $t=0$, calculate the position $x$ of the particle at time $t>0.$
questions.worked_solution:
We start by integrating the acceleration to get the velocity $v(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int 4{e}^{4t}\text{d}t \\  & ={e}^{4t}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(0)=1.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & ={e}^{4t}+C \\ 1 & ={e}^{4(0)}+C \\ 1 & =1+C \\ C & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So the velocity is given by $v(t)={e}^{4t}.$ 

Now, we integrate the velocity to get $x(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int {e}^{4t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{e}^{4t}+K\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $K,$ we use the fact that $x(0)=\frac{1}{2}.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} & =\frac{1}{4}{e}^{4t}+K \\ \frac{1}{2} & =\frac{1}{4}{e}^{4(0)}+K \\ \frac{1}{2} & =\frac{1}{4}+K \\ K & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the position $x$ of the particle at time $t$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\frac{1}{4}{e}^{4t}+\frac{1}{4} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{4t}+1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration $a(t)=\frac{1}{{t}^{2}},$ where $t\ge 1$ is the time. If the particle has position $x=4$ and velocity $v=0$ when $t=1,$ calculate the position $x$ of the particle at time $t\ge 1.$
questions.worked_solution:
We start by integrating the acceleration to get the velocity $v(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int \frac{1}{{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =-\frac{1}{t}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(1)=0.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =-\frac{1}{1}+C \\ C & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

So the velocity is given by $v(t)=-\frac{1}{t}+1.$

Now, we integrate the velocity to get $x(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int (-\frac{1}{t}+1)\text{d}t \\  & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡t+t+K\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $K,$ we use the fact that $x(1)=4.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}4 & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡(1)+1+K \\ 4 & =-0+1+K \\ K & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the position $x$ of the particle at time $t$ is 

$$
x(t)=-\operatorname{ln}⁡t+t+3.
$$

canonical_examples.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with velocity $v(t) = 2t+3t^2,$ where $t\geq 0$ is the time. If the particle is at the position $x=1$ when $t=0,$ calculate the position $x$ of the particle at time $t.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We start by integrating the velocity to get $x(t)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int (2t+3{t}^{2})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={t}^{2}+{t}^{3}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $x(0) = 1.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =(0)^{2}+(0)^{3}+C \\ C & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the position $x$ of the particle at time $t$ is

$$
x(t) = t^3+t^2+1.
$$

canonical_examples.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration $a(t) = 1-2t,$ where $t\geq 0$ is the time. If the particle has position $x=1$ and velocity $v=2$ when $t=1,$ calculate the position $x$ of the particle at time $t >0.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We start by integrating the acceleration to get the velocity $v(t)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int (1-2t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =t-{t}^{2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(1) = 2.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2 & =(1)-(1)^{2}+C \\ C & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

So the velocity is given by $v(t) = t-t^2 + 2.$

Now, we integrate the velocity to get $x(t)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int (t-{t}^{2}+2)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{t}^{2}-\frac{1}{3}{t}^{3}+2t+K\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $K,$ we use the fact that $x(1) = 1.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =\frac{1}{2}(1)^{2}-\frac{1}{3}(1)^{3}+2(1)+K \\ K & =-\frac{7}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the position $x$ of the particle at time $t$ is 

$$
x(t) = \dfrac{1}{2}t^2-\dfrac{1}{3}t^3 +2t -\dfrac{7}{6}.
$$
